Genesis.about: The book of beginnings. Chapters 1 to 11 tell of creation, the first sin and its spread, the flood and the tower of Babel: true teaching about God and humanity told in ancient story form. From chapter 12 God begins his rescue plan by choosing one family: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
Genesis.look: Watch how God keeps his promises even when people fail, and how he keeps choosing the younger and weaker.
Genesis.christ: The promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent (3:15), Abraham's sacrifice of his only son (22), and Joseph, rejected by his brothers and then saving them, all point to Jesus.
outline: The fall and the spread of sin
pray: Where in today's reading do you see God keeping a promise?
Which person in today's story is most like you right now?

Exodus.about: God hears his people crying in slavery in Egypt and frees them through Moses. He makes a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, gives the Ten Commandments, and comes to live among them in the tabernacle.
Exodus.look: Notice the pattern: God frees his people first, then gives them his law, then comes to dwell with them.
Exodus.christ: The Passover lamb whose blood saves (12) is the background of the Mass. The manna in the desert (16) points to the Eucharist, the bread from heaven.
outline: Slavery in Egypt and the call of Moses
The Passover and the crossing of the sea
The covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments
The golden calf and God's mercy
pray: What has God freed you from on your journey?
Where do you see God's patience with his people today?

Leviticus.about: The handbook for Israel's worship and holiness: sacrifices, priests, feasts and rules for clean living. It can feel strange to a modern reader, but its heart is one line: "Be holy, because I am holy."
Leviticus.look: Don't get lost in the details. Ask what each law taught Israel about God's holiness and about sin.
Leviticus.christ: The many sacrifices point to the one perfect sacrifice of Jesus. The Day of Atonement (16) is explained in the Letter to the Hebrews as a picture of Christ our High Priest.
pray: What does it mean for you to be holy in ordinary life?
What do you want to offer God today?

Numbers.about: Forty years in the desert. Israel is counted (that's the name), sets out from Sinai, complains, rebels, and is refused entry to the promised land for a generation. Yet God keeps feeding, guiding and forgiving them.
Numbers.look: Look for the grumbling and God's response. Notice the priestly blessing in chapter 6, still prayed today.
Numbers.christ: The bronze serpent lifted up so that those who look at it live (21) is used by Jesus himself for his cross (John 3:14).
outline: The people are counted at Sinai
The spies and forty years in the desert
pray: What do you grumble about? Bring it to God honestly.
How has God fed you in a desert time?

Deuteronomy.about: Moses' farewell speeches before Israel enters the land. He retells their story, repeats the law (the name means "second law"), and calls the people to choose life by loving God with their whole heart.
Deuteronomy.look: Find the Shema in chapter 6, the prayer Jesus calls the first commandment. Listen for the words "remember" and "choose."
Deuteronomy.christ: Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like him (18:15). Jesus quotes Deuteronomy three times when he is tempted in the desert.
outline: The Ten Commandments and the great commandment
Laws for life in the land
pray: What do you need to remember about God's goodness to you?
What does it mean to love God with all your heart today?

Joshua.about: Joshua, Moses' successor, leads Israel across the Jordan into the promised land. The walls of Jericho fall, the land is divided among the tribes, and Joshua calls the people to serve the Lord alone.
Joshua.look: The battles are hard reading. Read them as the story of God fulfilling his promise and of Israel's faithfulness or failure. Chapter 24 is the heart.
Joshua.christ: Joshua and Jesus are the same name in Hebrew: "the Lord saves." Joshua leads God's people into the land; Jesus leads us into the kingdom.
outline: The land divided among the tribes
Joshua's farewell and the covenant renewed
pray: "As for me and my house we will serve thee, Lord" (24:15). What would that look like in your home?
Where do you need courage, like Joshua?

Judges.about: After Joshua, Israel falls into a cycle: the people forget God, enemies oppress them, they cry out, God raises a judge to rescue them, and then they forget again. Deborah, Gideon and Samson are among the judges.
Judges.look: Track the cycle each time it repeats. The last chapters show how dark things get when "every one did that which seemed right to himself."
Judges.christ: Each judge is a flawed and temporary rescuer. The book makes you long for a true and faithful deliverer.
outline: The judges, from Othoniel to Deborah
pray: What pattern do you notice in your own turning away and coming back to God?
When have you cried out to God and been rescued?

Ruth.about: A short, beautiful story of loyalty. Ruth, a foreigner from Moab, refuses to leave her widowed mother in law Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Boaz, a kind relative, redeems and marries her.
Ruth.look: Notice the quiet kindness of ordinary people, and how God works without any miracles.
Ruth.christ: Ruth becomes the great grandmother of King David and appears in Jesus' family tree (Matthew 1:5). Boaz the redeemer is a picture of Christ.
outline: Naomi and Ruth return to Bethlehem
pray: Ruth chose a new people and a new God. How does her story speak to your own journey into the Church?
Who has shown you faithful kindness?

1 Samuel.about: Israel moves from judges to kings. The boy Samuel hears God's call in the night and becomes a prophet. The people demand a king, Saul is chosen and fails, and God sends Samuel to anoint the shepherd boy David.
1 Samuel.look: Watch how God looks at the heart, not the outside (16:7). In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 1 Kings.
1 Samuel.christ: David, the anointed shepherd king from Bethlehem, is the ancestor and picture of Jesus, the Messiah (the name means "anointed one").
outline: Hannah and the birth of Samuel
Saul's jealousy, David on the run
pray: Pray Samuel's words: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth."
Where do you judge by appearances instead of the heart?

2 Samuel.about: David's reign. He becomes king of all Israel, makes Jerusalem his capital, and receives God's promise of a kingdom that lasts forever (7). Then he falls into adultery and murder, repents, and suffers the sorrow of his family's troubles.
2 Samuel.look: Read chapter 12 with Psalm 50 (51 in modern Bibles), David's prayer of repentance. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 2 Kings.
2 Samuel.christ: God's promise to David (7:12-16) is fulfilled in Jesus, whom the angel calls heir to "the throne of David his father."
outline: David mourns Saul and becomes king
pray: David was a great sinner and a great repenter. What does his story say to you?
What does it mean that God builds you a "house"?

1 Kings.about: Solomon builds the Temple and is famous for wisdom, but turns to other gods in old age. The kingdom splits in two: Israel in the north, Judah in the south. The prophet Elijah stands against the worship of Baal.
1 Kings.look: Look for the prophets. Elijah on Mount Carmel (18) and hearing God in the quiet whisper (19) are high points. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 3 Kings.
1 Kings.christ: Jesus says "a greater than Solomon is here." Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration.
outline: The Temple is built and dedicated
pray: Solomon asked for a wise and listening heart. What would you ask God for?
Where do you need to listen for God in the quiet?

2 Kings.about: The two kingdoms go downhill. Elijah is taken up to heaven and Elisha continues his work. The northern kingdom falls to Assyria. A few good kings like Hezekiah and Josiah bring reform, but Judah falls to Babylon and Jerusalem is destroyed.
2 Kings.look: Each king is judged by one question: did he do what was right in the sight of the Lord? In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 4 Kings.
2 Kings.christ: Elisha's miracles, like multiplying bread (4:42-44) and healing Naaman in the Jordan (5), are echoed by Jesus.
outline: The fall of the northern kingdom
Josiah finds the book of the law
pray: Naaman had to wash in an ordinary river to be healed. Where might God be inviting you to humility?
What would it mean for you to do what is right in the sight of the Lord this week?

1 Chronicles.about: Written after the exile, Chronicles retells Israel's history with a focus on David, the Temple and true worship. It opens with long family lists that connect the returned exiles to Adam and to God's promises.
1 Chronicles.look: Skim the genealogies in chapters 1 to 9 with a prayer for your own family. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 1 Paralipomenon ("things left out").
1 Chronicles.christ: The focus on David's line and God's house prepares for Jesus, Son of David, who calls his body the new Temple.
pray: Pray for your ancestors and your family by name.
How do you take part in worship at Mass?

2 Chronicles.about: From Solomon's Temple to the exile, focusing on the kings of Judah. Faithful kings bring blessing; unfaithful ones bring ruin. It ends with hope: Cyrus of Persia lets the exiles go home to rebuild.
2 Chronicles.look: Notice God's promise in 7:14: if my people turn, pray and seek my face, I will hear from heaven and heal their land. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 2 Paralipomenon.
2 Chronicles.christ: The glory of God filling the Temple (5 to 7) points to God dwelling among us in Jesus.
outline: Exile and the decree of Cyrus
pray: "I will hear from heaven... and will heal their land" (7:14). Pray today for Canada.
What needs rebuilding in your life?

Ezra.about: The exiles return from Babylon to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple despite opposition. Ezra the priest-scribe arrives later and calls the people back to God's law.
Ezra.look: Notice the mix of joy and tears when the foundations are laid (3). In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 1 Esdras.
Ezra.christ: The return from exile is a picture of the greater homecoming Jesus brings: from sin back to the Father.
outline: The first return and the altar
pray: What does coming home to God feel like for you?
Where do you face opposition in rebuilding your faith?

Nehemiah.about: Nehemiah, a Jewish official in the Persian court, prays, then returns to rebuild Jerusalem's walls in just 52 days. Ezra reads the law aloud to the people, who weep and then celebrate.
Nehemiah.look: Nehemiah prays before every step. Chapter 8 is a beautiful scene of the people hearing God's Word. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 2 Esdras.
Nehemiah.christ: "The joy of the Lord is our strength" (8:10). The Liturgy of the Word at Mass continues this scene of God's people listening together.
pray: Nehemiah prayed a quick prayer before speaking to the king (2:4). Try that today.
How do you listen to God's Word at Mass?

Tobit.kind: Historical books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
Tobit.about: A warm family story. Tobit, a faithful Jew in exile, goes blind. His son Tobias travels to collect a debt, guided by a companion who turns out to be the archangel Raphael. Along the way Tobias marries Sara and Tobit is healed.
Tobit.look: See how prayer, almsgiving and care for the dead are honoured. Tobias and Sara's wedding night prayer (8) is often read at Catholic weddings. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called Tobias.
Tobit.christ: Raphael's name means "God heals." God is present and guiding even when we do not recognize it, as on the road to Emmaus.
pray: Who has been a Raphael for you, a guide sent by God?
Pray Tobias and Sara's prayer for a marriage you know.

Judith.kind: Historical books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
Judith.about: When a great army besieges a Jewish town and its leaders give up hope, the widow Judith, a woman of prayer and courage, goes into the enemy camp and defeats the general Holofernes. The book is a story told to strengthen faith.
Judith.look: Notice Judith's long prayer before she acts (9) and her rebuke of the leaders who tried to set deadlines for God (8).
Judith.christ: The Church has seen in Judith a picture of Mary, the woman through whom God defeats evil. Words said of Judith (15:10) are used in Marian feasts.
pray: Where are you tempted to give God a deadline?
What courage do you need to ask for today?

Esther.about: A young Jewish woman becomes queen of Persia and risks her life to save her people from a plot to destroy them. The Feast of Purim celebrates this rescue.
Esther.look: In the Douay-Rheims, chapters 10:4 to 16 are the Greek additions (including the prayers of Mordecai and Esther, 13 to 14), placed at the end as Saint Jerome arranged them.
Esther.christ: Esther, who intercedes for her people before the king, is a picture of Mary's intercession and of Christ who lays down his life for his people.
outline: Mordecai: "in such a time as this"
The Greek additions: dream, prayers and letters
pray: "That thou mightest be ready in such a time as this" (4:14). Why might God have placed you where you are?
Pray Esther's prayer in chapter 14 when you feel alone.

Job.about: Why do good people suffer? Job, a just man, loses everything. His friends insist he must have sinned; Job insists he has not and demands an answer from God. God finally speaks from the whirlwind, not with an explanation but by revealing himself.
Job.look: Most of the book is poetry. Don't take the friends' speeches as God's answer: at the end God says they did not speak rightly.
Job.christ: Job, the innocent sufferer, points to Jesus. His cry "I know that my Redeemer liveth" (19:25) is sung at funerals.
outline: Job and his three friends argue
pray: Bring an honest question or complaint to God today, as Job did.
When has God answered you with his presence rather than an explanation?

Psalms.about: The prayer book of Israel and of Jesus: 150 songs of praise, thanksgiving, sorrow, anger, trust and longing. Every human feeling is here, turned toward God. The Church prays the Psalms every day in the Liturgy of the Hours, and one is sung at every Mass.
Psalms.look: Pray them, don't just read them. The Douay-Rheims follows the old Latin numbering, so from Psalm 10 to 147 the number is usually one lower than in a modern Bible: "The Lord is my shepherd" is Psalm 23 at Mass and Psalm 22 here, where it begins "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing."
Psalms.christ: Jesus prays the Psalms on the cross (21 and 30 here; 22 and 31 in modern Bibles). Psalms 2, 109 and others are quoted in the New Testament as speaking of the Messiah.
pray: Choose one verse from today's psalms and repeat it through the day.
Which psalm today matches how you feel? Pray it as your own.

Proverbs.about: Short sayings for wise everyday living: work, words, money, friendship, family and self control. Its foundation: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out in the streets.
Proverbs.look: Read slowly and pick one saying a day to carry with you. The poem of the valiant woman closes the book (31).
Proverbs.christ: Wisdom present with God at creation (8) is read by the Church as pointing to Christ, the Wisdom of God.
outline: Agur and Lamuel; the valiant woman
pray: Which saying today touches your daily life?
Where do you need wisdom this week?

Ecclesiastes.about: A searching, honest book. The Preacher tries pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom, and finds everything "vanity": a breath that does not last. His answer: enjoy God's gifts simply, and fear God.
Ecclesiastes.look: Don't be put off by the gloom. The book clears away false hopes so we look for meaning in God alone. Chapter 3 ("a time to be born and a time to die") is famous.
Ecclesiastes.christ: The longing this book leaves is answered by Jesus, who gives life that does not pass away.
pray: What do you chase that doesn't satisfy?
What "time" are you in right now (3:1-8)?

Song of Songs.about: A love poem between a bride and her beloved. It celebrates human love as good and holy. Jews and Christians have also read it as the love between God and his people, and between Christ and the soul.
Song of Songs.look: Read it as poetry. Many saints, like Bernard of Clairvaux and John of the Cross, loved this book. In the Douay-Rheims it is called the Canticle of Canticles.
Song of Songs.christ: Christ is the Bridegroom and the Church is his Bride. "Love is strong as death" (8:6) finds its fullness on the cross.
pray: How does it feel to be loved by God like a beloved?
Pray: "I to my beloved, and my beloved to me."

Wisdom.kind: Wisdom books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
Wisdom.about: Written in Greek not long before Christ. It teaches that the souls of the just are in the hand of God (3), praises Wisdom as God's gift, and reflects on God's care for Israel in the Exodus.
Wisdom.look: Chapter 3:1-9 is often read at funerals. Chapter 2 describes the just man persecuted by the wicked, in words that fit Jesus' Passion.
Wisdom.christ: Wisdom is called "the brightness of eternal light" and "image of his goodness" (7:26), words the New Testament uses for Christ.
pray: Pray for someone who has died, trusting they are in God's hand (3:1).
Ask God for wisdom, as Solomon did (9).

Sirach.kind: Wisdom books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
Sirach.about: The longest wisdom book: practical teaching on prayer, friendship, family, speech, money and humility, from a teacher in Jerusalem about 180 years before Christ. It ends by praising Israel's great ancestors.
Sirach.look: It was used so much to teach new Christians that it got the name Ecclesiasticus, "the church book," which is its name in the Douay-Rheims.
Sirach.christ: Wisdom pitches her tent in Israel (24), as the Word "dwelt among us."
outline: Wisdom and the fear of the Lord
pray: Who is a faithful friend to you, "a strong defence" (6:14)? Thank God for them.
Which practical teaching today do you need?

Isaiah.about: One of the greatest prophets. Isaiah sees God's holiness in the Temple (6), warns Judah of judgment, and announces hope: a child called Emmanuel, a righteous king, a suffering servant, and a new creation.
Isaiah.look: Isaiah is so full of Christ it has been called the fifth Gospel. Look for the Advent and Christmas readings (7, 9, 11, 40) and the Good Friday servant song (53).
Isaiah.christ: "A virgin shall conceive" (7:14), "a child is born to us" (9:6), the servant wounded for our sins (53). Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 to announce his mission.
pray: "Here am I, send me" (6:8). Where might God be sending you?
Which promise of comfort in today's reading do you need?

Jeremiah.about: The weeping prophet. Called as a young man, Jeremiah warns Judah for forty years before the fall of Jerusalem. He suffers rejection, prison and despair, yet announces a new covenant written on the heart.
Jeremiah.look: Jeremiah's honest complaints to God (his "confessions," 11 to 20) show that we can pray even our pain.
Jeremiah.christ: The new covenant (31:31-34) is fulfilled at the Last Supper. Jeremiah, the rejected prophet who suffers for his people, is a picture of Jesus.
outline: The book of consolation and the new covenant
pray: "Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee" (1:5). Let God say this to you.
What pain do you need to bring to God honestly?

Lamentations.about: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction. In the middle of the sorrow comes the great act of hope: God's mercies are new every morning (3:22-23).
Lamentations.look: The poems are acrostics, following the Hebrew alphabet. The Church sings them in Holy Week.
Lamentations.christ: "O all ye that pass by the way, attend, and see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow" (1:12) is applied to Jesus on the cross and Mary at its foot.
outline: Hope in the middle of grief
pray: Is there a loss you have not grieved with God?
Pray 3:22-23 when you wake up tomorrow.

Baruch.kind: The Prophets (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
Baruch.about: Baruch was Jeremiah's secretary. The book offers a prayer of confession for the exiles, a poem praising Wisdom as God's law, and words of comfort for Jerusalem. Chapter 6 is the Letter of Jeremiah against idols.
Baruch.look: Chapter 3:9 to 4:4 is read at the Easter Vigil.
Baruch.christ: Wisdom "was seen upon earth, and conversed with men" (3:38), a line the Fathers saw fulfilled in Jesus.
pray: What "idols" compete for your heart?
Pray the confession in chapter 1 for your community.

Ezekiel.about: A priest taken to Babylon in exile, Ezekiel sees God's glory leave the Temple and later return. He acts out strange signs, promises a new heart and a new spirit, and sees dry bones come to life.
Ezekiel.look: Begin with the vision of God's glory (1), the good shepherd (34), the new heart (36) and the dry bones (37). The water flowing from the Temple (47) is read in Eastertide.
Ezekiel.christ: God promises to shepherd his sheep himself (34). Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd." Water flows from his side like the Temple river.
outline: The vision of God's glory and Ezekiel's call
Hope: the shepherd, the new heart, the dry bones
pray: "I will give you a new heart" (36:26). What in your heart needs to be made new?
Where in your life do things feel like dry bones?

Daniel.about: Daniel and his friends stay faithful in the court of Babylon: the fiery furnace, the lions' den, the writing on the wall. The second half contains visions of empires and of "one like the Son of man" given an everlasting kingdom.
Daniel.look: The Greek sections are included: the Song of the Three Young Men (3:24-90), Susanna (13) and Bel and the Dragon (14). The song is prayed in the Liturgy of the Hours.
Daniel.christ: Jesus calls himself the Son of Man, taking the title from Daniel 7:13-14.
outline: The fiery furnace and the song of the three
Visions and the Son of Man
pray: Where do you need courage to stay faithful in a culture that doesn't share your faith?
Pray the song of praise in chapter 3 today.

Hosea.about: God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, who will be unfaithful, as a living picture of God's love for unfaithful Israel. God's love wounds but never gives up: "I will espouse thee to me for ever" (2:19).
Hosea.look: Feel the emotion in chapter 11, where God speaks like a parent who taught a child to walk. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called Osee.
Hosea.christ: "I called my son out of Egypt" (11:1) is applied to Jesus in Matthew. Jesus quotes "I desired mercy and not sacrifice" (6:6).
pray: How does God's faithful love meet you in your unfaithfulness?
Hear God say to you, "I will heal their breaches, I will love them freely" (14:5).

Joel.about: A plague of locusts becomes a call to repent: "rend your hearts, and not your garments" (2:13), read on Ash Wednesday. Then God promises to pour out his Spirit on all flesh.
Joel.look: Peter quotes Joel's promise of the Spirit in his Pentecost sermon (Acts 2).
Joel.christ: The outpouring of the Spirit is fulfilled at Pentecost, after Jesus' Resurrection.
outline: Return to the Lord; the Spirit poured out
pray: What would it mean to rend your heart, not your garments?
Ask the Holy Spirit to fill you today.

Amos.about: A shepherd from the south sent to the rich north. Amos thunders against those who sold "the poor man for a pair of shoes" (2:6) while keeping up religious feasts. God wants justice to flow like water.
Amos.look: Notice how worship and justice belong together. Amos 9 ends with hope of restoration.
Amos.christ: Amos prepares for Jesus' care for the poor and his warning about the last judgment (Matthew 25).
outline: Judgment on the nations and Israel
pray: Who are the poor near you, and how is God asking you to act?
Does your worship lead to justice?

Obadiah.about: The shortest book of the Old Testament: one chapter against Edom, which rejoiced when Jerusalem fell. Pride and cruelty to a brother will be judged, and the kingdom will be the Lord's.
Obadiah.look: Edom descends from Esau, Jacob's brother. This is a story about brothers. In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Abdias.
Obadiah.christ: "The kingdom shall be for the Lord" (verse 21), the kingdom Jesus announces.
outline: Edom's pride and the day of the Lord
pray: Is there pride in you that rejoices at another's fall?
Pray for someone you are in conflict with.

Jonah.about: A prophet runs away from God, is swallowed by a great fish, prays, is spit out, preaches in Nineveh, and then sulks when God forgives Nineveh. A short story about God's mercy for everyone, even our enemies.
Jonah.look: Notice the ending: it is a question. God's mercy is wider than Jonah's.
Jonah.christ: Jesus points to the sign of Jonah: three days in the belly of the fish, as he would be three days in the tomb.
pray: Where are you running from what God asks?
Is there someone you don't want God to forgive?

Micah.about: A prophet from the countryside who speaks against injustice in Jerusalem. He sums up God's will: "to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God" (6:8). He also names Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace. In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Micheas.
Micah.look: Chapter 6:3-5 is sung on Good Friday as the Reproaches: "O my people, what have I done to thee?"
Micah.christ: "And thou Bethlehem Ephrata... out of thee shall he come forth" (5:2), quoted when the Magi come looking for Jesus.
outline: The mountain of the Lord; Bethlehem
pray: Which of the three in 6:8 is hardest for you right now?
Pray 7:18-19: God casts our sins into the depths of the sea.

Nahum.about: A poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh, the cruel capital of Assyria. For the oppressed, God's justice is good news.
Nahum.look: Read it alongside Jonah: Nineveh once repented, but later returned to cruelty.
Nahum.christ: "Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings" (1:15), echoed in the Gospel's good news.
outline: The Lord is a jealous God and a refuge
pray: Pray for people living under cruelty or war.
"The Lord is good, and giveth strength in the day of trouble" (1:7). Rest in that.

Habakkuk.about: A prophet argues with God: why do the wicked win? God answers, "the just shall live in his faith" (2:4). The book ends with a song of trust even if everything fails.
Habakkuk.look: The final verses (3:17-19) are one of the strongest prayers of faith in the Bible. In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Habacuc.
Habakkuk.christ: Saint Paul builds his teaching on faith on 2:4 (Romans 1:17).
outline: The just shall live by faith
pray: Pray 3:17-18 with your own list of what is missing in your life.
What question do you want to ask God?

Zephaniah.about: The day of the Lord is coming, a day of judgment on pride. But a humble remnant will be saved, and God will rejoice over his people with singing (3:17). In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Sophonias.
Zephaniah.look: The "Dies irae" hymn draws on 1:15. The joy of 3:14-18 is read in Advent.
Zephaniah.christ: "Give praise, O daughter of Sion" (3:14) echoes in the angel's greeting to Mary.
pray: Let God rejoice over you today (3:17).
What does humility look like for you?

Haggai.about: After the exile, people rebuild their own houses but leave God's house in ruins. Haggai urges them to put God first and promises the new Temple will be filled with glory. In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Aggeus.
Haggai.look: Two short chapters with one message: consider your ways.
Haggai.christ: The promise of greater glory in the new Temple (2:10) is fulfilled when Jesus enters it.
pray: What gets your time before God does?
Where does God want to be first in your week?

Zechariah.about: A prophet of the return from exile who encourages rebuilding through night visions. The second half speaks of a humble king, a shepherd struck down, and one "whom they have pierced." In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Zacharias.
Zechariah.look: Chapters 9 to 14 are quoted many times in the Gospel accounts of Holy Week.
Zechariah.christ: "Behold thy king will come to thee... he is poor, and riding upon an ass" (9:9), Palm Sunday. "They shall look upon me, whom they have pierced" (12:10), the cross.
outline: The one they pierced; the Lord is king
pray: How is Jesus a king unlike the kings of the world?
Look at a crucifix and pray 12:10.

Malachi.about: The last book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles. Malachi calls priests and people back to sincere worship and faithful marriage, and promises a messenger to prepare the Lord's way, Elijah before the great day. In the Douay-Rheims the book is called Malachias.
Malachi.look: "From the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice" (1:11) is echoed in the Eucharistic Prayer.
Malachi.christ: The messenger is John the Baptist, who prepares the way for Jesus. The pure offering everywhere is the Mass.
outline: The messenger and the Lord's coming
The day of the Lord and Elijah
pray: How do you prepare your heart for Mass?
Who has been a messenger preparing the way of the Lord for you?

1 Maccabees.kind: Historical books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
1 Maccabees.about: About 170 years before Christ, a Greek king tries to wipe out Jewish faith. The priest Mattathias and his sons, led by Judas Maccabeus, resist, purify the Temple (remembered at Hanukkah), and win independence.
1 Maccabees.look: Watch how faithfulness costs something real. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 1 Machabees.
1 Maccabees.christ: The rededication of the Temple is the Feast of Dedication that Jesus attends in John 10:22, where he says he is the one the Father consecrated.
pray: What does faithfulness cost you today?
Pray for Christians persecuted for their faith.

2 Maccabees.kind: Historical books (one of the seven books found in Catholic Bibles)
2 Maccabees.about: A second account of the same struggle, told to inspire faith. It includes the martyrdom of the elderly Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons, who die hoping in the resurrection.
2 Maccabees.look: Chapter 7 is one of the clearest Old Testament witnesses to the resurrection of the body. Chapter 12 shows prayer for the dead. In the Douay-Rheims this book is called 2 Machabees.
2 Maccabees.christ: The martyrs' hope in being raised by God prepares for Jesus' Resurrection.
outline: Letters to the Jews in Egypt
The martyrs Eleazar and the seven brothers
pray: Pray for someone who has died, as Judas did (12:46).
What does the mother's courage in chapter 7 say to you?

Matthew.about: Written for Jewish Christians, Matthew shows Jesus as the promised Messiah, Son of David, who fulfills the Law and the Prophets. His Gospel gathers Jesus' teaching into five great sermons, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount.
Matthew.look: Watch for "that it might be fulfilled": Matthew links Jesus to Old Testament promises again and again. It is the Gospel of the Church: only Matthew records "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church" (16:18).
Matthew.christ: Matthew begins with Emmanuel, "God with us" (1:23), and ends with Jesus' promise "I am with you all days" (28:20).
outline: John the Baptist and the temptation
Miracles and the mission of the Twelve
Peter's confession and the way of the cross
The Resurrection and the Great Commission
pray: Which words of Jesus today do you want to put into practice?
Picture yourself in today's scene. What does Jesus say to you?

Mark.about: The shortest and probably the first Gospel, traditionally linked to Peter's preaching in Rome. Mark moves fast and shows Jesus in action. The question at its heart: who is this man? The answer comes from a Roman soldier at the cross: "Indeed this man was the son of God."
Mark.look: Notice how often the disciples misunderstand. Mark is honest about their weakness, and that gives us hope.
Mark.christ: The whole book answers Jesus' question in 8:29: "Whom do you say that I am?"
outline: Peter's confession and the road to Jerusalem
pray: What surprises you about Jesus in today's reading?
Where are you, like the disciples, slow to understand?

Luke.about: Written by a companion of Paul for a Gentile reader, Luke is the Gospel of mercy, prayer, the poor, women and the Holy Spirit. Only Luke tells of the Annunciation, the shepherds, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son and the road to Emmaus.
Luke.look: Notice how often Jesus prays, and how he welcomes outsiders. Luke gave the Church three daily prayers: the canticles of Mary, Zechariah and Simeon.
Luke.christ: Jesus is the Saviour of all. Luke's long journey to Jerusalem (9 to 19) is a path of discipleship we walk too.
outline: The births of John and Jesus
John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism
pray: Who are the outsiders Jesus welcomes in today's reading? Who are they in your life?
Pray with one line from today the way Mary pondered in her heart.

John.about: The beloved disciple's Gospel, the most reflective of the four. John begins before creation, "In the beginning was the Word," and tells seven signs and seven "I am" sayings. He spends five chapters on the Last Supper.
John.look: Look for the signs (water into wine, the bread of life, the man born blind, Lazarus) and what they reveal. John wrote "that you may believe" (20:31).
John.christ: "The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (1:14). Jesus is the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection, the way, the true vine.
pray: Which "I am" of Jesus do you need today?
Hear Jesus ask you, as he asked Peter: "Lovest thou me?"

Acts.about: Luke's second volume: the story of the Church from Jesus' Ascension and Pentecost to Paul preaching in Rome. The Holy Spirit is the main character, driving the Gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
Acts.look: Notice the sacraments in action: Baptism, the laying on of hands, the breaking of bread. Watch Peter in the first half and Paul in the second.
Acts.christ: The risen Jesus keeps working through his Church. Saul hears him say, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest" (9:5): Christ and his Church are one.
outline: Paul arrested and sent to Rome
pray: Where do you see the Holy Spirit at work in today's reading, and in your life?
Pray for your parish to be like the first community (2:42).

Romans.about: Paul's greatest letter, written to a church he had not yet visited. All have sinned, and all are saved not by their own effort but by God's grace through faith in Christ. Then he shows what life in the Spirit looks like.
Romans.look: Chapter 8 is one of the high points of the Bible: nothing "shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus" (8:39). Chapter 12 turns teaching into daily life.
Romans.christ: Christ is the new Adam who undoes the first Adam's sin (5).
pray: What does it mean to you that nothing can separate you from God's love (8:38-39)?
Offer yourself to God today as a living sacrifice (12:1).

1 Corinthians.about: Paul writes to a gifted but divided church in a busy port city. He addresses factions, sexual morality, marriage, food offered to idols, the Eucharist, spiritual gifts and the resurrection.
1 Corinthians.look: Chapter 11 has the earliest written account of the Last Supper. Chapter 13 is the hymn to love. Chapter 15 is the oldest summary of the Resurrection.
1 Corinthians.christ: "We preach Christ crucified" (1:23). We are the Body of Christ, and "the bread which we break, is it not the partaking of the body of the Lord?" (10:16).
outline: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
Freedom and food offered to idols
pray: Where are you tempted to divide rather than unite?
Read 13:4-7 and ask God where to grow in love.

2 Corinthians.about: Paul's most personal letter. Hurt by conflict with the Corinthians, he opens his heart about his sufferings and weakness, and about the ministry of reconciliation God has given to the Church.
2 Corinthians.look: Look for the theme of strength in weakness: "My grace is sufficient for thee" (12:9).
2 Corinthians.christ: "God indeed was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself" (5:19). This is the heart of the sacrament of Reconciliation.
outline: The ministry of the new covenant
Paul defends his ministry; strength in weakness
pray: Bring your weakness to God and hear, "My grace is sufficient for thee."
With whom do you need to be reconciled?

Galatians.about: A passionate letter to churches tempted to think Gentile Christians must keep the whole Jewish law. Paul insists we are saved by faith in Christ and freed to live by the Spirit.
Galatians.look: Find the fruits of the Spirit in 5:22-23. "I live, now not I, but Christ liveth in me" (2:20) sums up the Christian life.
Galatians.christ: "God sent his Son, made of a woman" (4:4), the earliest mention of Mary in the New Testament.
outline: Faith, the law and the promise to Abraham
Freedom and the fruit of the Spirit
pray: Which fruit of the Spirit (5:22-23) do you most need?
What would it mean for Christ to live in you today?

Ephesians.about: Paul writes from prison about God's great plan to unite all things in Christ, and about the Church as Christ's Body and Bride. Then he shows how this changes daily life, family life and spiritual battle.
Ephesians.look: Chapter 1 is a hymn of blessing. Chapter 5 compares marriage to Christ's love for the Church. Chapter 6 describes the armour of God.
Ephesians.christ: Christ is the head of the Church, his Body, and "he is our peace" who breaks down every dividing wall (2:14).
outline: Saved by grace; one new people
Christ and the Church; family life
pray: Pray Paul's prayer in 3:14-19 for someone you love.
Which piece of the armour of God do you need today?

Philippians.about: A letter of joy written from prison to a church Paul loved. He shares the hymn of Christ who emptied himself and was exalted, and encourages them to rejoice, pray and not worry.
Philippians.look: The word "joy" or "rejoice" appears again and again. Chapter 2:6-11 is one of the earliest Christian hymns.
Philippians.christ: Christ "emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" and became obedient unto death on a cross (2:7-8).
pray: Pray 4:6-7: bring every worry to God with thanksgiving.
What does it mean to have the mind of Christ (2:5)?

Colossians.about: Paul writes to a church tempted by new philosophies and spiritual practices. Christ is enough: he is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation, and the head of the Church.
Colossians.look: The hymn in 1:15-20 is a high point. Chapter 3 shows how to "put on" the new life.
Colossians.christ: "In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally" (2:9).
pray: What would it mean to "seek the things that are above" (3:1) today?
Which virtue in 3:12-14 do you want to put on?

1 Thessalonians.about: Probably the oldest book of the New Testament. Paul encourages a young, persecuted church, thanks God for their faith, and answers their question about believers who have died before Christ's return.
1 Thessalonians.look: Short, warm and practical. "Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks" (5:17-18).
1 Thessalonians.christ: Christ will come again, and those who died in him will rise (4:13-18).
outline: Holy living and hope for the dead
The day of the Lord; final advice
pray: Practise 5:16-18 today: rejoice, pray, give thanks.
Pray for someone you love who has died, in the hope of 4:13-14.

2 Thessalonians.about: A short follow-up. Some thought the day of the Lord had already come and stopped working. Paul corrects them: stay steady, hold to the traditions you were taught, and work quietly.
2 Thessalonians.look: "Hold the traditions which you have learned, whether by word, or by our epistle" (2:14) shows tradition alongside Scripture.
2 Thessalonians.christ: The Lord Jesus will come in glory and is faithful to strengthen us (3:3).
pray: Ask God to direct your heart "in the charity of God, and the patience of Christ" (3:5).
Where do you need steadiness instead of anxiety?

1 Timothy.about: Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in Ephesus, about healthy teaching, prayer for all people, the qualities of bishops and deacons, care of widows, and the danger of loving money.
1 Timothy.look: God "will have all men to be saved" (2:4). The Church is "the pillar and ground of the truth" (3:15).
1 Timothy.christ: There is "one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (2:5).
outline: Sound teaching and Paul's story of mercy
pray: Pray for leaders, as 2:1-2 asks.
Paul calls himself the chief of sinners who found mercy (1:15). How does that speak to you?

2 Timothy.about: Paul's last letter, written in chains as he waits for death. He urges Timothy to guard the faith, to suffer bravely, to keep reading Scripture and to preach in season and out of season.
2 Timothy.look: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (4:7). Paul's farewell.
2 Timothy.christ: "Be mindful that the Lord Jesus Christ is risen again from the dead" (2:8).
outline: Hard times and the power of Scripture
pray: Who handed the faith on to you, like Timothy's grandmother and mother (1:5)? Thank God for them.
What would it mean for you to "finish the course" (4:7)?

Titus.about: Paul's instructions to Titus, leading the church on the island of Crete: appoint good leaders, teach sound doctrine, and live in a way that makes the Gospel attractive.
Titus.look: Chapter 3:4-7 is a beautiful summary of salvation through "the laver of regeneration": Baptism.
Titus.christ: "The grace of God our Saviour hath appeared to all men" (2:11), read at Christmas.
pray: How does your life make the Gospel attractive to others?
Thank God for the mercy of Baptism (3:5).

Philemon.about: A one-page personal letter. Onesimus, a runaway slave, has become a Christian through Paul. Paul sends him back to his master Philemon and asks him to welcome Onesimus "Not now as a servant, but instead of a servant, a most dear brother" (16).
Philemon.look: Read it in one sitting. It shows how the Gospel changes relationships from the inside.
Philemon.christ: Paul offers to pay Onesimus' debt himself: a picture of Christ who takes our debt on himself.
pray: Who do you need to see as a brother or sister in Christ?
Is there someone you need to welcome back?

Hebrews.about: A powerful sermon to Jewish Christians tempted to go back to the old ways. Jesus is greater than the angels, than Moses and than the old priesthood. He is the eternal High Priest who offered himself once for all.
Hebrews.look: Chapter 11 is the great "hall of faith" of Old Testament heroes. Chapter 12 calls us to run with our eyes on Jesus.
Hebrews.christ: Jesus is our High Priest who sympathizes with our weakness (4:15), the mediator of a better covenant, and the one perfect sacrifice made present at every Mass.
outline: The Son greater than the angels
The new covenant and the perfect sacrifice
pray: Bring a weakness to Jesus, our High Priest who can "have compassion on our infirmities" (4:15).
Which hero of faith in chapter 11 inspires you?

James.about: Practical wisdom for Christians: be doers of the word and not hearers only. Faith without works is dead. Watch your tongue, care for the poor, and don't favour the rich.
James.look: Chapter 5:14-15 is the scriptural basis for the Anointing of the Sick.
James.christ: James was a relative of Jesus and leader of the church in Jerusalem. His letter echoes the Sermon on the Mount.
outline: Trials, wisdom and doing the word
pray: What word have you heard that you need to do?
Pray for someone who is sick, as 5:14-16 asks.

1 Peter.about: Peter writes from Rome to scattered Christians facing suffering. He reminds them of their Baptism and new birth, their dignity as "a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood," and how to suffer well, following Christ.
1 Peter.look: It sounds like a Baptism homily. Be "ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason of that hope which is in you" (3:15).
1 Peter.christ: "By whose stripes you were healed" (2:24), quoting Isaiah 53. Christ went to preach to the spirits in prison (3:19), which we profess in the Creed: he descended to the dead.
outline: Born again to a living hope
A chosen people; following Christ's example
pray: What is the reason for the hope in you? Try putting it into words.
Cast your care on God, for he cares for you (5:7).

2 Peter.about: A farewell letter warning against false teachers and scoffers who say Christ will never return. Peter remembers the Transfiguration and reminds us that God is patient, not wanting anyone to perish.
2 Peter.look: "Partakers of the divine nature" (1:4) is one of the boldest lines in Scripture about what grace does.
2 Peter.christ: Peter was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain (1:16-18).
pray: Which virtue in the ladder of 1:5-7 is your next step?
Thank God for his patience with you (3:9).

1 John.about: A letter from the beloved disciple about how to know we truly belong to God: walk in the light, keep his commandments, believe that Jesus came in the flesh, and above all love one another. "God is charity."
1 John.look: It circles around three themes: light, love and truth. Read slowly.
1 John.christ: "In this is charity: not as though we had loved God, but because he hath first loved us, and sent his Son" (4:10).
outline: Keep his commandments; abide in him
Children of God love one another
pray: "God is charity" (4:16). Rest in that today.
Bring your sins to God, trusting 1:9.

2 John.about: A very short letter to "the lady elect and her children," probably a local church. Walk in love and in the truth, and do not welcome teaching that denies Jesus came in the flesh.
2 John.look: Read it in one sitting, along with 3 John.
2 John.christ: Jesus Christ truly "is come in the flesh" (verse 7).
pray: How do truth and love go together in your relationships?

3 John.about: A short personal note to Gaius, praising his hospitality to travelling missionaries and warning against Diotrephes, who loves to be first.
3 John.look: A window into the everyday life of the early Church.
3 John.christ: Welcoming those who go out "for his name" (verse 7) is serving Christ.
pray: Who could you welcome or support in their service of the Gospel?

Jude.about: A short, urgent letter to "contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints" against those twisting God's grace into an excuse for sin. It ends with one of the most beautiful doxologies in the Bible.
Jude.christ: Christ is able to keep you from stumbling and present you spotless before his glory (verse 24).
pray: Pray verses 20-21: build yourself up, pray in the Spirit, keep yourself in God's love.

Revelation.about: John, exiled on the island of Patmos, receives visions of the risen Christ, the heavenly worship around the Lamb, the struggle between good and evil, and the final victory: a new heaven and a new earth. Written to give hope to persecuted Christians.
Revelation.look: Don't read it as a puzzle of dates. It is a book of worship and hope, full of symbols from the Old Testament. Much of the Mass, like the "Holy, Holy, Holy" and the Lamb, is here. In the Douay-Rheims it is called the Apocalypse.
Revelation.christ: Christ is the Lamb who was slain and now reigns. "Behold, I make all things new" (21:5).
outline: The vision of the risen Christ
Worship in heaven and the Lamb
The wedding feast of the Lamb
A new heaven and a new earth
pray: Join the worship of heaven: pray "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty" (4:8).
What do you want God to make new?
